title: External conditions alone cannot explain complex coadaptations

fields.label: Label
fields.value: External conditions alone cannot explain complex coadaptations

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Complex adaptations and coadaptations between organisms, such as the woodpecker's feeding structures or the misseltoe's dependence on particular trees, birds and insects, cannot be accounted for by the direct effects of external conditions such as climate and food.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it is preposterous to attribute to mere external conditions, the structure, for instance, of the woodpecker, with its feet, tail, beak, and tongue, so admirably adapted to catch insects under the bark of trees.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), the Introduction; section “Introduction”. Scope: adapted structures of animals and plants, especially those involving relations with other species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-intro-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Morphology, interactions and some common-garden data are public, but no integrated dataset spans complex adaptations generally. Restricted comparative tests are feasible, while excluding every external-condition account is difficult.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across well-studied structures, partition phenotypic variation into direct environmental plasticity and evolved, heritable effects, and test whether climate or food alone predicts complex functional matching. Persistence of matching after common-environment and phylogenetic controls would refute the proposed external-only explanation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical causes are confounded with present-day function.

The universal scope cannot be exhaustively sampled.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Climate layers, trait compilations, and interaction records exist and can support a residual test for some well-known plant-animal systems. They do not cover the full range of coadapted structures, and several plausible mappings from Darwin's wording onto variables compete. Even a large residual for biotic partners would leave room for correlated selection and unmeasured food variables, so the result would be informative mainly for particular systems.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit trait and interaction models for coadapted structures (foraging morphology, host and pollinator links) against climate- and diet-only models. The external-conditions account would be supported if climate and food variables left little residual association between the coadapted traits and the partner organisms; it would be weakened if biotic partners explained that structure after climate and phylogeny were controlled.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
What counts as a complex coadaptation, and as fully accounting for it, has to be stipulated before any model comparison is decisive.

Quantitative functional morphology for animals such as woodpeckers is scattered, so most tests would use a biased subset of well-studied interactions.

Phylogenetic inertia and historical biogeography produce trait-environment correlations that mimic a direct climatic explanation.
